frames.narration: The query arrives: orders joined to customers, WHERE country = 'US'. The parser checks the syntax, resolves the names and builds a logical plan: scan customers, filter, join to orders. Nothing says yet how.

The optimiser cannot run candidates to find out, so it asks the statistics. customers has 1,000 rows and US is 40% of them, so it expects 400. orders has 20,000 rows over 1,000 customers, about 20 each, so the join should return about 8,000 rows.

It costs each join method. Nested loop compares 400 x 20,000 rows: cost about 20,435. Merge join must sort 20,000 orders first: about 1,204. Hash join builds a table from 400 customers and streams orders through it: about 558. The cheapest wins.

The executor runs the plan. It scans customers (25 pages), keeps the 400 US rows in a hash table, then scans orders (200 pages) and probes the table once per order. In total 225 pages are read sequentially.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports the result: 7,795 rows against the 8,000 estimated, and a real cost of 558. Estimated and actual rows agree within a few percent, so the plan was a good choice for the right reasons.
Weeks later a bulk load has multiplied the tables and nobody ran ANALYZE. The statistics still describe a world 20 times smaller where this country was rare (0.2%).
Planning the same query, the optimiser now expects 1 customer row. With one outer row, a nested loop looks cheapest: cost 238 against 242 for the hash join. It picks the nested loop.

At run time 400 customers match, not 1. The executor compares each of them with all 20,000 orders: 8,000,000 comparisons, real cost about 20,435, around 37 times the 558 of the hash join. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows it: estimated rows 1, actual rows 400.
Running ANALYZE resamples the tables. The statistics now say 400 US customers, the optimiser picks the hash join again and the query is back to a cost of 558.
